title: Track 7, Lesson 9: Common psychological mistakes - FOMO and confirmation bias
subtitle: Investors usually lose to their own psychology rather than to a lack of analytical knowledge.
whyItMatters: Knowing these traps in advance helps you notice when you are falling into one yourself, rather than reading about them as other people's problem - a skill for protecting your money that matters as much as analysis.
openingQuestion: What behaviour does FOMO (fear of missing out) usually lead to in investing?
openingOptions: Doing very thorough research and full data analysis before making any investment decision at all
Buying simply because the price is rising and you fear missing out
Selling a profitable holding immediately to lock in gains, regardless of its long-term growth prospects
Staying away from the stock market entirely in all circumstances, on the view that investing is always too risky
explanation: FOMO makes investors buy with the crowd once the price has already risen a long way (usually near a peak), out of fear of 'missing out' rather than judging whether the asset is still attractive at today's price. It is one of the most common reasons retail investors buy at the top and sell at the bottom.

diagram.label: The price rises sharply, near a peak
FOMO: fear of missing out, buying with the crowd
Never reassessing whether the price still makes sense

realWorldExample.description: During a hot run in any asset (shares, cryptocurrency), the number of new investors joining usually spikes exactly when the price has already risen a great deal - many of them buying near the peak out of FOMO, and taking heavy losses when it corrects.

quiz.question: What is confirmation bias in investing?
options: A tendency to believe whatever you read most recently
Seeking only information that supports what you already think
A tendency to sell as soon as the first loss appears
A tendency to follow the majority in the wider market
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias leads an investor who has bought a share to read only positive news about it and skip the risk warnings - reinforcing a mistaken belief and delaying recognition of the problem until the damage is large.

quiz.question: You bought share X believing its growth story. News then emerges that the company is in serious difficulty, but you read only the optimistic analysis and skip the bad news. Which bias is this, and what is the sensible remedy?
options: Herd behaviour - stop following investment groups
Loss aversion - set an automatic stop-loss order
Confirmation bias - deliberately read the opposing view
Anchoring - reset your reference price
quiz.explanation: A textbook case of confirmation bias: taking in only what reinforces an existing belief. The practical remedy is to actively seek out and seriously weigh the opposing view, asking "what would prove me wrong" instead of hunting for evidence that supports the decision already made.

quiz.question: What is the most common mistake FOMO causes?
options: Splitting a portfolio across so many tickers that none of them can be followed
Selling far too early, as soon as an investment shows a small gain
Holding cash too long and missing an entire market upswing
Buying after a sharp rise out of fear of missing out, rather than on analysis
quiz.explanation: The order gets reversed: instead of analysing then deciding, people see the price rise and then look for a reason to justify it. This is why retail money flows in most heavily just before a peak.

quiz.question: How does confirmation bias show up in investing?
options: Reading only information that supports a decision already made
Investing only in companies many experts have confirmed to be good
Buying shares only after confirmation from the brokerage firm
Trusting only financial statements confirmed by an independent audit
quiz.explanation: After buying, you start reading the good news more carefully than the bad, and seeking out communities that hold the same ticker. The defence is writing down in advance what would make you admit you were wrong - before you buy.

quiz.question: Why does 'anchoring' keep investors holding a losing share?
options: Taking the share's all-time high price as the target for selling
Taking your purchase price as the anchor, waiting to break even
Taking the brokerage's recommended price as the decision point
Taking the sector average price as the benchmark for the holding
quiz.explanation: The market does not know what you paid and does not care. The right question is always: with what I know today, would I buy this at the current price - if not, the only reason to hold is the anchor.

quiz.question: What most effectively reduces the impact of these biases?
options: Investing only on the recommendations of highly experienced experts
Following the market much more closely so that you can react quickly to every price move
Writing down your rules and reasons in advance, then checking decisions against them
Waiting until you feel completely certain before committing any money
quiz.explanation: Biases work hardest when you decide while the market is moving. A rule written down while calm is the only thing that stands up to the panicking version of yourself.

keyTakeaways: FOMO makes investors buy with the crowd near a peak out of fear of missing out, not on any assessment of value
Confirmation bias makes investors seek only information supporting a decision already made, ignoring warning signs
The practical remedy: deliberately seek out the opposing view before deciding, rather than believing only what you want to believe

practicePrompt.question: You bought share Y believing its long-term growth story. A recent analyst report flags rising debt as a risk, but you read only the pieces praising the company and skip that report. Which bias is this?
options: Confirmation bias: seeking and believing only what supports a decision already made, and ignoring the contrary view
This is FOMO (fear of missing an opportunity), and has nothing whatsoever to do with which information you choose to read and trust
This is a sensible investment strategy, because concentrating on positive information helps maintain conviction in the investment
This is not a bias of any kind, but simply a preference for reading positive news rather than negative news
practicePrompt.explanation: Actively reading the opposing or negative view before deciding whether to hold or sell is the remedy for confirmation bias - rather than believing only what you want to believe.

summary.keyIdea: FOMO makes investors buy with the crowd near a peak out of fear of missing out, not on any assessment of value
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Confirmation bias makes investors seek only information supporting a decision already made, ignoring warning signs

application.title: Test yourself
application.message: Think back to your most recent investment decision - did you actively look for the opposing view before deciding, or only read what supported what you already wanted to believe?
application.secondary: Being honest in that answer is how you start noticing your own biases.

sections.text: Most retail investors do not lose for want of analytical knowledge - they lose to psychology. The two most common biases are FOMO (fear of missing out) and confirmation bias, and both steer decisions quietly, without your noticing.
FOMO: buying with the crowd near the peak

FOMO makes investors buy once the price has already risen sharply - usually near a peak - out of fear of 'missing' the opportunity, rather than judging whether the asset is still attractive at today's price. During hot runs in shares or cryptocurrency, the number of new investors joining spikes exactly when the price has already risen a great deal - many of them buying near the top and taking heavy losses in the correction. It is one of the most common reasons retail investors buy the top and sell the bottom.
Confirmation bias: hearing only what you want to hear

Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and believe information that supports an existing view, while ignoring or discounting anything contrary. **Example:** you bought share X believing its growth story. News then emerges that the company is in serious difficulty, but you read only the optimistic analysis and skip the bad news - reinforcing a mistaken belief and delaying recognition of the problem until the damage is large.

The remedy for confirmation bias is to actively seek out the contrary or negative views on your own investment and weigh them fairly before deciding to hold or sell, rather than hunting for evidence supporting the decision already made. A useful question to ask yourself: 'What would prove me wrong?' - if you cannot answer it, confirmation bias is very likely running the decision.

items: Before buying because a price is surging, ask: 'Would I buy at this price if I didn't know it had just risen?'
Deliberately find at least one contrary analysis before every large investment decision
Write down your original reason for buying and periodically check whether it still holds
Set a minimum thinking time before buying into a market frenzy - never decide within minutes
Distinguish clearly between 'I believe in the company' and 'I believe the price will keep rising' - these are two different beliefs
